transcript:
For the final module of this course, we are going to go over the current recommendations and solutions that exist in the world as of today, so you may be aware of what is already taking place and how you may get involved.

To begin, we are going to dive into the research recommendations and theoretical frameworks that have been created to guide generative AI development and integration. Much of the research that has been included in this course comes with a range of calls to actions, whether it be to parents/caregivers, educators, policy makers, or AI developers. Many of these recommendations focus on establishing stronger AI literacy in schools, as it can be one of the first places a child can encounter generative AI. Recommendations to educators and those in charge of curriculums have similar themes involving risk mitigation and proactive action. However, it must be noted that amongst all of the research reviewed for the development of this course, none of them mentioned removing or blocking AI from education.

One repeated recommendation was the implementation of designated AI literacy programs in school, whether it is integrated through existing courses [1] or have designated orientations or courses [2]. For course integration, recommendations vary depending on the core intent of AI literacy from the proposer. For instance, if the intent is to promote healthy AI interaction to reduce dependency, then one call to action recommends starting a beginning-of-term AI orientation, hosting AI literacy workshops for families and students, and designing assignments in a way to reduce the option for AI overreliance, such as oral exams [2]. If the intention is to address ethical AI tool designs as early as possible, then another call to action recommends integrating the concept of anthropomorphism and its effects into computer science classrooms so future AI developers may understand the considerations surrounding generative AI [1].

Another repeated recommendation is implementing specific strategies into teaching curricula to curb the damage generative AI use can cause, both directly and subtly. Some activities include:

[1] Students are presented with examples of anthropomorphically designed tools and are taught the pros and cons of these design choices, with the intent to persuade students to use these tools with this lens in mind. [1]

[2] Students are presented with examples of anthropomorphic statements, such as “ChatGPT knows what I am thinking” and asked to debunk them with explanations on how generative AI tools are designed, with the intent to train students to recognize cues that chatbots use to develop trust and dependency. [3]

[3] Students are presented with examples of AI-generated outputs that have a varying degree of hallucination or misinformation, with the intent to highlight to students that inaccurate statements can be produced from these models. [4]

[4] Students role play different stakeholders in generative AI design and how they are affected by certain design choices, both positively and negatively, with the intent to make students think critically about ethical considerations. [1]

[5] Students review AI output for bias, with the intent to disrupt the belief that AI tools are perfect. [5]

[6] Students are more often given assignments that promote critical thinking and reviewing diverse sources, with the intent to build up these researching skills and understand how these AI tools work and can make mistakes

[7] Students should discuss the possible pitfalls of using generative AI tools whenever they are given an assignment that allows for their use. [6]

[8] Students should be taught the inner workings of generative AI, such as how its algorithms work, to demystify these tools and reduce the perception that these tools are perfect. [2]

Finally, many pieces of research call for the augmentation of current teaching principles to thoughtfully integrate AI, instead of haphazardly allowing students access to generative AI. These recommendations include the implementation of educational strategies that prioritize cognitive skill and critical thinking by emphasizing active engagement, and creating extra emphasis on why the hard parts of learning, such as struggle and challenging, is a good thing [7]. 

Additionally, the role of AI should be made extremely clear: it is a supporting tool, and not a one-stop-shop for finishing assignments. Educators can highlight strategies of using AI tools, such as communicating with it for brainstorming, working on a problem without receiving an explicit answer, and working on ideas, while also prompting students to come up with their own ideas first and to critique every output from the tool [6]. These recommendations also call for the school itself to get involved by conducting reviews of how AI is being utilized and creating scaffolding for assignments that may integrate AI tools [2].

These recommendations attempt to mitigate generative AI harm by addressing ethical and informational concerns through already implemented learning institutions, in hopes of addressing these points while children and adolescents are still developing their relationships with AI and themselves. By making explicit and subtle changes to the school curriculum, a great amount of proactive work can be done to protect younger generations from being hurt. However, these recommendations are not exclusive to schools, and many can be implemented at home or other environments.
